title: Z-Function and Pattern Matching
summary: The Z-array records, for every position, how far it matches the string's own prefix — an O(n) construction that powers substring search plus period and border problems that KMP's LPS array doesn't directly answer.

slides.markdown:
The **Z-array** answers one question for every position `i` in a string: "how many characters starting at `i` match the string's own prefix?" That single array, built in O(n), turns out to solve substring search as cleanly as KMP's LPS array does — and it directly exposes two things KMP's array doesn't: every **period** of the string, and every **border** (a prefix that's also a suffix), without extra derivation.

This is the same core idea as [naive-pattern-matching-and-kmp](naive-pattern-matching-and-kmp) approached from a different angle: instead of matching the pattern against itself to build a fallback table, you match the *whole concatenated string* against its own prefix directly.

For a string `s` of length n, `Z[i]` (for `i > 0`) is the length of the longest substring starting at `i` that matches a prefix of `s`. By convention `Z[0]` is left undefined or set to 0/n depending on the source — it's never used in the pattern-matching application.

For `s = "aabxaabxcaabxaabxay"`, `Z[4] = 4` because `s[4:8] = "aabx"` matches the prefix `"aabx"` exactly, and no longer match extends further (position 8 is `'c'`, breaking the match).

The pattern-matching use: build `combined = pattern + separator + text` and compute its Z-array. Any position where `Z[i] == len(pattern)` marks a spot in the text where the pattern occurs — a match is literally "this position matches the whole prefix," and the prefix is exactly the pattern you're searching for.

![The Z-array below each character of the string, with the current rightmost matched span bracketed as the active Z-box](assets/z-function-array-zbox.svg)

The Z-box is the bookkeeping that makes construction O(n): it's the rightmost-reaching match window found so far, `[l, r]`. When computing `Z[i]` for an `i` inside an existing Z-box, you can reuse the already-known match length from the mirrored position instead of comparing characters from scratch — exactly the same spirit as KMP reusing the LPS array.

slides.sectionTitle: Using the Z-array for pattern search
slides.markdown:
```python
def z_search(text, pattern):
    combined = pattern + '#' + text   # '#' must not appear in either string
    z = z_array(combined)
    m = len(pattern)
    return [i - m - 1 for i in range(m + 1, len(combined)) if z[i] == m]
```

The separator is what prevents the pattern from "matching into" the text side accidentally — without it, a Z-value could legitimately extend across the pattern/text boundary and produce a false positive. Every reported index is adjusted back to the text's own coordinate space by subtracting `m + 1` (the pattern length plus the separator).

slides.sectionTitle: A separator that appears in the input
slides.markdown:
If the chosen separator character actually occurs somewhere in the pattern or the text, the Z-array can produce matches that extend across the pattern/text boundary — corrupting the count and reporting false or missing matches near where the separator collided with real data.

A common, mostly-safe choice is a character outside the expected alphabet — `'#'`, `'\0'`, or `'\x01'` for lowercase-letter problems. But "mostly safe" is not "provably safe": if the input is genuinely arbitrary bytes, you need a separator you can *guarantee* doesn't appear, which sometimes means scanning the input first or using a value outside the byte range entirely (e.g., pairing characters with an out-of-band marker instead of concatenation).

| | Z-array | KMP's LPS array |
|---|---|---|
| What it stores per index i | Match length between position i and the string's prefix | Match length between a prefix and a suffix ending at i |
| Built over | pattern + separator + text (one combined string) | The pattern alone |
| Construction | O(n), via the Z-box reuse trick | O(m), via self-referential fallback |
| Extra problems solved directly | Periods, borders, longest common prefix of two strings | Requires re-deriving from the LPS values |

Both are O(n) and both solve substring search — the practical choice is often just familiarity, though the Z-array's separate-pattern-from-text setup makes it marginally more natural for the period/border family of problems, since those are properties of one string matched against itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Periods and borders from the Z-array
slides.markdown:
A **period** of a string is a prefix length `p` such that repeating that prefix (possibly with a partial final repeat) reconstructs the whole string — `"abcabcab"` has period 3, since `"abc"` repeated (and truncated) gives it back.

The Z-array exposes periods directly: `p` is a period of `s` (length n) exactly when `p + Z[p] == n` — meaning the match starting at position `p` runs all the way to the end of the string. Scanning the Z-array for every index satisfying this gives you every period in one O(n) pass.

A **border** (a proper prefix that's also a proper suffix — the same concept KMP's LPS array tracks) is closely related: `s` has a border of length `n - p` for every period `p` found this way. Counting distinct periods and counting distinct borders are, practically, the same scan.

The same `pattern + separator + text` trick generalizes to comparing any two strings: build `A + separator + B` and the Z-array immediately gives you, for every position in B, how long a prefix of A it shares — which is exactly the longest-common-prefix machinery behind problems like finding the longest common substring of two strings (combined with a suffix-array-style approach) or checking string rotations.

This reuse is the practical payoff of learning the Z-array on top of KMP rather than instead of it: the same one array construction answers substring search, period-finding, border-finding, and prefix-comparison-between-two-strings, where KMP's LPS array is more narrowly tuned to the single-pattern search it was built for.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this fits in the string toolkit
slides.markdown:
Big picture: KMP, Rabin-Karp, and the Z-function all solve exact substring search in linear time, using three genuinely different mechanisms — a self-referential fallback table, a numeric rolling hash, and a self-comparison array. Knowing more than one isn't redundant: an interviewer asking "how would you find every period of this string" is really asking for the Z-array specifically, since deriving periods from KMP's LPS array takes an extra logical step that the Z-array skips.

The next topics in this group — suffix arrays and Manacher's algorithm — build on this same family of ideas: self-comparison structures that trade a different kind of bookkeeping for the same O(n) or O(n log n) guarantees on string problems.
